lessons.title: The New Tax Regime: The Default Option, Its Slabs and the Rebate

children.text: If you never tell your employer or the tax department anything, you are already in the new regime. That is what default means. So before you judge whether to leave it, you need to know exactly what it gives you: seven slabs, a ₹75,000 standard deduction and a rebate big enough to make ₹12.75 lakh of salary tax-free.

body.caption: New Tax Regime Slabs, Tax Year 2026-27 (Resident Individuals, All Ages)
headers: Total tax at top of band

body.text: Every band is exactly ₹4 lakh wide and each step adds 5 percentage points. Memorise that pattern and you can calculate new regime tax in your head. The last column is your shortcut: find the band, take the total at the top of the band below, and add the rate on whatever sits above it.

markDefs.definition: The rate that applies to your next rupee of income, that is, the rate of the highest slab your income reaches.
Your total tax divided by your total income. Always lower than the marginal rate in a slab system.

points: "I'm in the 20% slab, so I pay 20% of my income as tax"
"A raise that pushes me into a higher slab will reduce my take-home"
"The ₹12 lakh limit means the first ₹12 lakh is always tax-free for everyone"

columns.label: What actually happens
points: Only income above ₹16 lakh is taxed at 20%. Your effective rate is far lower
Higher rates apply only to the extra income, and marginal relief protects you near ₹12 lakh
The rebate is all or nothing. Cross ₹12 lakh of taxable income and slab tax applies from ₹4 lakh upward

body.title: Slab Practice
body.prompt: Meera, a product manager in Gurugram, has taxable income of ₹22,00,000 under the new regime. What is her total tax including 4% cess?
body.explanation: Total tax at ₹20 lakh is ₹2,00,000. The next ₹2,00,000 falls in the 25% band, adding ₹50,000. Slab tax is ₹2,50,000. Cess at 4% is ₹10,000. Total: ₹2,60,000.

children.text: Salaried employees and pensioners get a flat ₹75,000 standard deduction under Section 19 of the Income-tax Act, 2025 (Section 16(ia) of the 1961 Act). No proof, no investment, no receipts. It simply comes off your salary before slabs are applied. Freelancers and business owners do not get it, because they deduct actual business expenses instead.

body.label: Salary that pays zero tax in the new regime
body.context: ₹12,00,000 rebate limit plus the ₹75,000 standard deduction. Applies to resident salaried individuals with no special-rate income.

children.text: The Rebate: Why ₹12 Lakh Is the Magic Number

Section 156 of the Income-tax Act, 2025 (Section 87A of the 1961 Act) gives resident individuals a rebate of up to ₹60,000 if their taxable income does not exceed ₹12 lakh. Look back at the slab table: tax at exactly ₹12 lakh is ₹60,000. The rebate is sized to cancel it completely. That is how the slabs start taxing income at ₹4 lakh while the effective tax-free limit sits at ₹12 lakh.

stats.label: Maximum rebate
stats.context: Equal to slab tax at ₹12 lakh

body.title: Rebate Check
body.question: Neha, a credit analyst at a Mumbai bank, has a salary of ₹12,60,000 and no other income. What is her tax under the new regime?
body.explanation: Salary of ₹12,60,000 minus the ₹75,000 standard deduction gives taxable income of ₹11,85,000. That is below ₹12 lakh, so the rebate cancels the slab tax of ₹58,500 in full. Tax is nil.

body.title: Remember the Limit
body.textWithBlank: In the new regime, the rebate is available only if taxable income does not exceed ₹___ lakh.
body.explanation: The limit applies to taxable income, after the standard deduction. For a salaried employee that corresponds to a salary of ₹12.75 lakh.

children.text: The Cliff Just Above ₹12 Lakh, and Marginal Relief

markDefs.definition: A cap that limits tax to the amount by which income exceeds a threshold, so that earning slightly more never leaves you with less money after tax.

children.text: The rebate is all or nothing. At ₹12,00,000 of taxable income you pay nil. At ₹12,10,000 the rebate vanishes and slab tax becomes ₹61,500. Earning ₹10,000 more would cost you ₹61,500. The law fixes this with
: your tax cannot exceed the amount by which your income crosses ₹12 lakh. At ₹12,10,000, tax is capped at ₹10,000, plus cess.

body.title: Show me where marginal relief ends

children.text: Marginal relief applies while normal slab tax is higher than the excess over ₹12 lakh. Call the excess x. Slab tax is ₹60,000 plus 15% of x. Relief stops when the two are equal:

content.caption: Marginal relief applies to taxable income from ₹12,00,001 to about ₹12,70,588, which is a salary of about ₹13,45,588.

children.text: Above that point, normal slab tax is already lower than the excess, so no relief is needed. Cess at 4% is charged on the tax after marginal relief.

body.title: Vikram's Appraisal Panic
body.scenario: Vikram, a software engineer at a Hyderabad GCC, earns ₹12,50,000 and pays no tax under the new regime. His appraisal letter raises him to ₹13,20,000. A colleague warns him that the ₹70,000 raise will push him out of the rebate and he will end up worse off.
body.prompt: Is the colleague right? Work out Vikram's new tax and what he actually gains.
body.modelAnswer: The colleague is wrong. New taxable income is ₹13,20,000 minus ₹75,000, which is ₹12,45,000. Normal slab tax is ₹60,000 plus 15% of ₹45,000 (₹6,750), total ₹66,750. The excess over ₹12 lakh is only ₹45,000, so marginal relief caps tax at ₹45,000. Add 4% cess of ₹1,800 for total tax of ₹46,800. His raise is ₹70,000, so he keeps ₹23,200 more than before. Marginal relief means a raise never leaves you with less money, although near the ₹12 lakh line much of the raise goes to tax.

body.title: Effective Tax Rate by Salary, New Regime

body.text: The rebate does not cover everything. Income taxed at special rates, such as short-term capital gains on listed shares sold on NSE or BSE (20%) and long-term capital gains above ₹1.25 lakh (12.5%), does not get the rebate. A salaried investor with ₹11 lakh of taxable salary and ₹1 lakh of short-term gains from a Zerodha account still pays tax on those gains. Chapter 3 works through this.
The new regime's real power is not its slab rates. It is the rebate. Up to ₹12.75 lakh of salary, no amount of deductions in the old regime can beat zero.

body.title: Calculate Your Own New Regime Tax
steps: Take your annual gross salary from your CTC breakup or last year's Form 16
Subtract the ₹75,000 standard deduction to get taxable income
If taxable income is ₹12 lakh or less, your tax on salary is nil. Stop here
Otherwise, use the 'total tax at top of band' column to find slab tax
Check whether marginal relief applies (taxable income up to about ₹12.7 lakh)
Add 4% cess and write down the number. You will compare it with the old regime in Chapter 3

points: The new regime has seven slabs, each ₹4 lakh wide, rising from nil to 30% above ₹24 lakh.
Slab rates apply only to the income inside each band, so your effective rate is always below your marginal rate.
Salaried employees get a ₹75,000 standard deduction under Section 19 (16(ia)) with no proofs needed.
The rebate under Section 156 (87A) cancels up to ₹60,000 of tax when taxable income is ₹12 lakh or less, making ₹12.75 lakh of salary tax-free.
Marginal relief caps tax at the amount by which income crosses ₹12 lakh, so a raise never leaves you worse off.
Special-rate income like capital gains on shares does not get the rebate, and NRIs cannot claim it.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not tax advice. Figures reflect the rules applicable to tax year 2026-27 as understood at the time of writing, for resident individuals without surcharge. Confirm against the latest Finance Act or a qualified tax professional before filing.
